hook: Starship Reaches *Orbit* for the First Time
dek: Starship reached orbit for the first time despite an engine loss and a scrub reversal.

slides.label: What Happened
slides.text: SpaceX's Starship launched from South Texas early Monday and reached *Earth orbit* for the first time ever.

slides.label: The Hiccup
slides.text: Right after stage separation, the upper stage lost *one of its six* Raptor engines.

slides.label: Quick Reversal
slides.text: SpaceX first called off the orbit attempt, then reversed course minutes later and kept pushing.

slides.label: The Plan
slides.text: The original plan: orbit Earth *six times* over nine hours while deploying *26* new Starlink satellites.

slides.label: Still Unclear
slides.text: It's still unclear if that mission plan changed because of the engine loss and the delay.

slides.label: Booster Landing
slides.text: The Super Heavy booster separated, returned to the Gulf coast, and stuck its *cleanest* simulated landing yet.

slides.label: Big Picture
slides.text: Musk is centering the whole company on Starship, from NASA moon missions to orbital data center satellites.

slides.label: Why It Matters
slides.text: Reusable rockets could cut launch costs, opening space work to *more builders*, not just legacy giants.

question: Would cheaper rockets open space up to more builders, not just billionaires?
caption_instagram:
Starship just made it to orbit, and it wasn't a clean ride.

SpaceX's mega rocket launched from South Texas early Monday and reached Earth orbit for the first time ever, according to TechCrunch. Right after stage separation, the upper stage lost one of its six Raptor engines. SpaceX first scrubbed the orbit attempt, then reversed course minutes later and kept pushing.

The original plan had Starship circling Earth six times over nine hours while dropping off 26 new Starlink satellites. It's still unclear if that plan changed. Meanwhile the Super Heavy booster nailed its cleanest simulated landing yet, a big step toward a fully reusable rocket.

Reaching orbit brings SpaceX closer to regular commercial missions and cheaper access to space, which could open doors for builders who never had a shot at the industry before.

Would cheaper rockets open space up to more builders, not just billionaires?
